claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are crystalline, solid, well dispersed, and elementally homogeneous.
Cu is the component of FeNiCrCoCu with the lowest melting point.
Heating FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles causes Cu to migrate preferentially to their surfaces.
Surface enrichment of Cu produces local structural disorder and a liquid-like surface layer.
Cu segregation lowers the local melting point at the nanoparticle surface.
The Cu-enriched liquid-like surface layer nucleates melting and promotes its propagation from the exterior into the particle interior.
A liquid-like surface phase will appear below the predicted bulk melting point.
Surface premelting will be followed by rapid melting throughout the particle.
Particles with enhanced surface Cu concentration will show an earlier and more pronounced surface-melting response than compositionally homogeneous baseline particles.
Particles with minimized surface segregation will melt more uniformly and at a higher temperature, with behavior closer to bulk melting.
Thermal exposure can drive segregation and microstructural evolution in high-entropy alloys.
Temperature-dependent changes can alter phase stability in multicomponent transition-metal high-entropy alloys.
Particle size, composition, heating rate, and degree of Cu segregation affect the premelting onset and melt-propagation rate.
Changes in particle size, atmosphere, or extreme heating rate may alter segregation dynamics and melting behavior.
